title: Testing the boundary
idea: MEET. The boundary (the exact cutoff value) is where >= vs > bugs live. Reason about which side of the line a value falls.

exercises.prompt: A rule says 'passes if score is 50 or more'. The BOUNDARY value to test is...
exercises.explanation: 50 is the exact cutoff. Testing 50 proves whether 'or more' really includes the boundary (it does: >=).

exercises.prompt: With rule 'score >= 50', does a score of exactly 50 pass?
exercises.explanation: >= includes the boundary, so 50 passes. If the code used >, 50 would wrongly fail — that's the classic boundary bug.

exercises.prompt: A rule says 'free coffee if the order is OVER 25'. Does an order of exactly 25 earn one?
exercises.explanation: 'Over' means strictly greater (>), so 25 does NOT qualify. Only 26 and up do. Words map to > vs >=.
options: No — 'over 25' is strict, so 25 does not qualify

exercises.prompt: Match the English phrase to the comparison it means.
exercises.explanation: English hides the boundary: 'at least'/'or more' is >=, 'over'/'more than' is >, 'under'/'less than' is <.

exercises.prompt: Testing exactly the boundary value is the best way to catch a > vs >= bug.
exercises.explanation: Yes — a value on the boundary is the ONLY input where > and >= disagree. That's why it's the key test.

exercises.prompt: To fully test 'score >= 50', which THREE values are most revealing?
exercises.explanation: 49 (just below), 50 (the boundary), 51 (just above) pin down exactly where the line is. The boundary trio.

exercises.prompt: A program counts 'adults (18+)'. Someone tests only ages 25 and 40. What's the risk?
exercises.explanation: Both are clearly adults, so the code never meets age 18 or 17 — the boundary where the rule actually matters is untested.
options: It never tests ages near 18, where the rule matters most

exercises.prompt: If 49, 50, and 51 all behave correctly, the >=/> choice is well tested.
exercises.explanation: Yes — those three straddle the boundary, so correct behaviour on all three confirms the comparison is right.

exercises.prompt: Why do boundary bugs survive casual testing?
exercises.explanation: Casual tests use 'obvious' values far from the line, so > and >= give the same answer and the bug stays hidden.
options: Values far from the boundary behave the same under > and >=

exercises.prompt: The habit this lesson builds is...
exercises.explanation: Whenever a rule has a cutoff, deliberately test the exact boundary and one value each side. That's rigorous checking.
options: Always test the exact cutoff and one value on each side
